buildSteps.title: Choose the modality, host and site
buildSteps.detail: A facility picks superconducting, trapped-ion, neutral-atom, photonic or annealing hardware and a building with stable power, low floor vibration and helium access — often alongside an existing national laboratory or supercomputing centre.

buildSteps.title: Prepare the lab environment
buildSteps.detail: RF-shielded rooms, clean spaces, cryogen plumbing, helium recovery lines, filtered electrical supplies and grounding are installed before any qubit hardware arrives.

buildSteps.title: Install cryogenics or vacuum systems
buildSteps.detail: Dilution refrigerators are assembled and leak-checked, or ion/atom vacuum chambers are baked and pumped down, and wiring looms are thermally anchored at every cooling stage.

buildSteps.title: Mount and wire the qubits
buildSteps.detail: Chips are bonded into shielded sample packages, connected to filtered microwave lines, and aligned in optical setups where lasers rather than microwaves do the work.

buildSteps.title: Bring up control electronics
buildSteps.detail: Racks of waveform generators, RF sources and digitizers are synchronised to nanosecond timing, and laser tables are locked to stable references.

buildSteps.title: Cool down and characterise
buildSteps.detail: The system is taken to base temperature over several days; wiring attenuation, crosstalk and qubit spectroscopy are checked before any external user touches it.

buildSteps.title: Calibrate and benchmark
buildSteps.detail: Single- and two-qubit gate fidelities, coherence times, readout error and connectivity are measured systematically and recorded as a machine-readable device profile.

buildSteps.title: Stand up the access layer
buildSteps.detail: A scheduler, cloud API, compiler stack, user authentication and quota accounting are layered on top, so remote jobs land on the same queue as local ones.

buildSteps.title: Operate, re-calibrate and publish
buildSteps.detail: Automated calibration runs daily, hardware is serviced on a cycle, and noise and benchmark datasets are released openly so outside groups can reproduce earlier claims.

prerequisites.why: superconducting qubits only work within a few thousandths of a degree of absolute zero, and helium supply and recovery must be reliable.

prerequisites.tech: Precision microwave, RF and laser control
prerequisites.why: qubit operations need phase-stable pulses with sub-nanosecond timing and readout of very weak signals.
shared access at scale is a solved pattern inherited from high-performance computing, once hardware is exposed as a service.
randomised benchmarking and related methods exist, but metrics are not yet consistent across modalities or facilities.
facilities today mostly rent out noisy physical qubits; only small error-corrected demonstrations have appeared.

pathway.milestone: national labs and supercomputing centres offer scheduled cloud access to in-house and commercial quantum processors
pathway.unlocks: startups and universities can test algorithms on real hardware and reproduce published performance claims.

pathway.milestone: common benchmarking standards and shared noise datasets across sites
pathway.unlocks: results become comparable across hardware generations and vendors rather than resting on self-reported figures.

pathway.milestone: quantum processors integrated directly into high-performance computing clusters with a single scheduler
pathway.unlocks: hybrid classical-quantum workflows where a simulation hands off to a quantum unit mid-job.

pathway.milestone: error-corrected processors and entanglement links between facilities
pathway.unlocks: testbeds become nodes in a distributed quantum network, and users gain dependable logical qubits instead of raw noisy ones.
